patient.chief_complaint: Seven-day rapidly progressive ascending paralysis and areflexia, preceded by diarrheal illness. SpO2 92% on room air — respiratory failure imminent.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. A. is a 28-year-old restaurant worker presenting with rapidly progressive ascending weakness over 7 days. He had bloody diarrhea 3 weeks ago, lasting 5 days, consistent with Campylobacter (no stool culture obtained but presentation classic). Seven days ago, he noticed tingling in his feet. Weakness ascended rapidly — he could not walk 3 days ago, and now cannot move his legs at all. Bilateral facial drooping developed 2 days ago. He is now in respiratory distress with SpO2 92% on room air and FVC 41%. He is being brought emergently for ICU level care.

specialized_test.impression: Very severe acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with features of secondary axonal injury. Markedly prolonged distal motor latencies, severely reduced conduction velocities, markedly reduced CMAP amplitudes, absent sural SNAPs, absent F-waves and H-reflex bilaterally. Findings meet electrodiagnostic criteria for acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: GBS prognostic factors
results.finding: EGOS (Erasmus GBS Outcome Score) predicts unaided walking at 6 months; axonal injury (low CMAP) is the strongest predictor of poor outcome

results.title: Severe GBS prognosis
results.finding: Patients requiring MV: 60-70% walk independently at 1 year; 15-20% have permanent disability; 5% mortality

output.summary: Published evidence indicates that severe GBS requiring mechanical ventilation is associated with 60–70% probability of independent walking at 1 year; 15–20% of patients sustain permanent disability; reported mortality is approximately 5%. High anti-GM1 titers and CMAP amplitude reduction (secondary axonal injury) are independently associated with slower and incomplete recovery. Extended inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation is typically required.

critical_actions: INTUBATE IMMEDIATELY — not a discussion, patient in respiratory failure (SpO2 92%, CO2 52)
DO NOT USE SUCCINYLCHOLINE — use rocuronium for RSI
ICU admission for temporary pacing capability — life-threatening bradycardia expected in severe GBS

key_reasoning_points: Most severe GBS case in series — respiratory failure present on arrival; CO2 52 and SpO2 92% demand immediate intubation before any other workup
Succinylcholine must not be used — in GBS, upregulated nicotinic receptors release massive potassium causing cardiac arrest; rocuronium is the RSI agent of choice
Temporary cardiac pacing required in severe GBS with autonomic arrest — must have transvenous pacing capability available
Very high anti-GM1/GD1a titers predict severe disease with axonal injury and prolonged recovery
GBS is NOT caused by corticosteroids or exacerbated by avoiding them — do not give steroids
